name: process-manager
intent: Coordinate a multi-step, message-driven flow from one place: a process manager keeps the state of the sequence, decides the next step from intermediate results, and owns the timeouts and compensations that the flow cannot get from a local transaction.
problem: A logical operation spans several steps and participants, the steps are not fully known at design time or are not sequential, and no distributed transaction is available: someone must remember where the flow is, decide what happens next from intermediate results, and undo already-completed steps when a later one fails - yet spreading that knowledge across the participants turns the flow into something no one can see, change or audit.
context: Message-driven integration or service boundary where one logical operation spans several services or steps and takes seconds to months: replies arrive asynchronously and must be matched to the running instance, the next step depends on what earlier steps returned, some steps may run in parallel, and the flow must continue correctly after a crash, a lost reply or a participant that never answers.
benefits: The flow lives in one place: sequence, branching, timeouts and compensation are explicit, reviewable and versionable instead of being inferred from scattered event handlers.
Decisions can use intermediate results, so conditional and parallel steps are expressible - the reason EIP contrasts it with Routing Slip, whose route must be fixed up front.
Participants stay independent: each receives a command and replies, and knows nothing about the overall flow, so a step can be reused, replaced or tested without touching the others.
Failures get a defined outcome: an outstanding request times out, the manager retries, skips or compensates, and the operation ends in a known state instead of hanging forever.
Operational visibility: the persisted instance state answers where a flow is and what it is waiting for, and a message history shows how it got there.
tradeoffs: Hub-and-spoke concentrates load and availability: every step round-trips through the coordinator, which EIP explicitly names as the danger of turning the process manager into a performance bottleneck; instances must be sharded by correlation key to scale.
The coordinator accretes business rules; unmanaged, it becomes a god workflow that every team has to change and no team owns.

Coordination needs durable state and reliable sends: unless the state transition and the outgoing command commit atomically (transactional outbox, transactional channel), the manager itself loses or duplicates steps.
Every step must be idempotent, because the same reply can be delivered twice and a command can be redelivered after a crash - exactly-once is not available.
Debugging spans the coordinator, the participants, the state store and the transport, so a fault can surface far from its cause.

Applied to a flow that a fixed linear route would handle, a process manager adds a permanent component, persistent storage and an extra hop for no coordination benefit (EIP: using one for every integration problem is overkill).

participants.responsibility: Owns the running flow: loads the instance state, decides the next step from (state, event), sends the resulting command or commands, persists the transition and arms any deadline it needs.
The durable record of one run - correlation key, current state, completed and pending steps, deadlines, collected data and process-definition version - which is the source of truth after a crash.
The command or business event that creates a process instance and fixes the correlation identifier used by every later message of that run.
An application service that performs one step on request and replies with a correlated result or error, without any knowledge of the flow it belongs to.
The result message the manager matches back to the waiting instance; duplicate and late replies must be tolerable by design, not by hope.
Fires when an outstanding request misses its deadline so the manager can retry, skip or compensate instead of waiting forever.
Undoes a completed step when the flow fails irrecoverably or a deadline passes; every irreversible action needs one, and they run in reverse completion order.
The versioned description of states, transitions, guards, deadlines and compensation mapping that the manager interprets for an instance of that version.

use_cases: Order fulfilment: reserve credit, reserve stock, take payment, arrange shipment - each step compensated in reverse order if a later one fails (the canonical saga scenario).
Loan broker (the EIP example): a request is fanned out to several banks, the manager waits for quotes under a deadline and returns the best offer or a timeout.
Travel booking: flight, hotel and car reservations chained conditionally, each with its own cancellation deadline and its own compensation.
Subscription dunning: retry payment on a schedule, downgrade or suspend on repeated failure, notify the customer - one long-lived instance per subscription.
Claim adjudication or employee onboarding where steps belong to different teams and hand-offs take days, so the flow must survive restarts and staff turnover.
Document or data pipelines whose next stage depends on the outcome of earlier stages, with a deadline that aborts the run when a stage stalls.
Temporal Workflows: durable, signal-driven executions coordinate Activities with persisted state, timers and Saga-style compensation for long-running business processes.
AWS Step Functions Standard Workflows: state machines coordinate Task, Parallel and Map states with Wait, Retry and Catch transitions when downstream work branches or fails.

Azure Durable Functions orchestrations: stateful orchestrators coordinate activities and sub-orchestrations, wait for external events or durable timers, and invoke compensating actions after failures.
avoid_when: The route is fixed, linear and known at design time: attach a Routing Slip and let the participants forward the message themselves.
The work fits one local transaction, or the interaction is a single request-reply with a retry: use the transaction or the Retry pattern.
Messages are independent and high-volume with no cross-step state: routing them costs less than coordinating them.
Choreography is a deliberate organisational choice - each team owning its reaction to domain events - and a central coordinator would reintroduce exactly the coupling that choice removed.
The only available artifact is a BPMN model nobody will maintain: flow state written and reviewed as code is easier to test and version than a diagram with a runtime nobody owns.
anti_patterns: God workflow: one process manager for every flow in the company, so each change queues behind its owning team and the hub becomes the release bottleneck.
In-memory process state: the manager works until the first restart, after which flows are lost or re-run with duplicated side effects.
Pretend distributed transaction: coordinating steps without idempotent participants and compensations, expecting two-phase-commit semantics that message delivery cannot provide.
Timeouts without compensation: reservations expire and stay held because no handler ever releases them.
Camouflaged orchestration: participants call each other in a fixed order while everyone claims the flow is choreographed, so nobody owns the sequence.
design_principles: Single responsibility: participants execute one step, the process manager owns the sequence - neither does the other's job.
Separation of concerns: flow logic stays out of the participants; business data stays out of the coordinator wherever possible.
Information hiding and low coupling: participants depend only on command and reply contracts, never on the flow definition.
Make state explicit: named states with guarded transitions instead of a scatter of boolean flags that only together mean something.
Fail-safe default: every outstanding request has a deadline and every irreversible action has a compensation.
Open/closed: new steps arrive as new transitions and participants, without editing the existing ones.
best_practices: Persist the transition atomically with the outgoing command (transactional outbox or transactional channel) so a crash cannot lose or duplicate a step.
Key every message by the business correlation identifier and make both commands and replies idempotent (Idempotent Receiver) - at-least-once delivery is the norm.
Give every outstanding request a deadline and a decided outcome: retry, skip or compensate, never wait indefinitely.
Design and test the compensation path as carefully as the happy path; compensations run in reverse order and must tolerate being run twice.
Keep the coordinator thin: pure decision functions over persisted state, with domain logic pushed into the participants.
Version the process definition and let a running instance finish on the version it started with; record that version in the instance state.
Make the flow observable: record transitions on the instance and publish them (Message History, Wire Tap) so support can see what an instance is waiting for.
Shard instances by correlation key and keep per-instance work serial; the hub must not become the only thread in the system.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Process Manager (Messaging Routing chapter, p. 312).
